name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 30 March 1968

clue.text: Daughterly birthday presents for Zeus? Naughty!

blocks.note: surface reading: what gifts would the king of the gods get from his daughters?
setter's reading: Zeus had nine daughters, the Muses, and if each gave him a tie the total sounds like a decade famed for naughtiness

explanation.surface: A playful question about what the daughters of Zeus might give him for his birthday.
explanation.walkthrough: Nine Muses each giving a tie make NINE TIES, and the Naughty Nineties is the familiar name for the 1890s.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1890s are popularly remembered as a decade of gaiety and loosened morals, hence the stock phrase Naughty Nineties.

clue.text: Signs of approval about Mum from travellers

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: nods of the head show approval
Ma is a familiar word for mother

explanation.surface: Wandering people nod their approval of someone's mother.
explanation.definitionFit: Nomads are wandering people with no fixed home who move from place to place, so they are travellers.

clue.text: Blood unfavourably compared with simple faith

definitions.text: Blood unfavourably compared with simple faith

blocks.clueFragment: Blood unfavourably compared with simple faith
blocks.note: surface reading: lineage judged worse than plain belief
setter's reading: Tennyson wrote that kind hearts are more than coronets, and simple faith than a particular kind of aristocratic blood

explanation.surface: A moral that noble lineage counts for less than plain trust.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is from Tennyson's Lady Clara Vere de Vere: 'Kind hearts are more than coronets, And simple faith than ___ blood.'
explanation.definitionFit: Descent from the Conquest-era invaders marked the oldest English aristocracy, which the poet ranks below sincerity.

clue.text: A French president makes her' sit awkwardly

indicators.note: done awkwardly means arranged clumsily, so the letters come out in a new order

blocks.note: the two words are the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A head of state in France makes a woman sit uncomfortably.
explanation.definitionFit: Adolphe Thiers was the first president of the French Third Republic, from 1871 to 1873.

clue.text: It's asking too much

blocks.note: surface reading: a complaint that a request is unreasonable
setter's reading: a description of a price far above what is fair

explanation.surface: A protest that a demand goes too far.
explanation.definitionFit: Prices or demands described this way are excessive, far beyond what is reasonable to charge or expect.

clue.text: Dandies discover skill in cryptic writings

indicators.note: something cryptic is obscured or scrambled, so these letters are not in their plain order
one piece is placed inside the other, as the word says

blocks.note: MSS is the abbreviation for manuscripts
art as in craft or skill

explanation.surface: Fashionable men find that cryptic writing takes real skill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cryptic writings' looks like a description of crosswords; 'cryptic' is the signal working on the manuscript abbreviation, and the skill sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A smart is an old term for a fashionable, well-dressed man about town, so the plural names such fops.

clue.text: The hermit - bird

blocks.note: first meaning: a Muslim holy man or recluse in North Africa
second meaning: an alternative spelling of the marabou, a large African stork

explanation.walkthrough: Hermit looks like it might be the hermit crab or hermit thrush, pointing to one creature; it is a separate meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a North African Muslim ascetic and a large carrion-eating stork.

clue.text: Remainder can be got from said rule

indicators.note: something got from other material is made out of it, so these letters are reworked into a new word

blocks.note: the two words are the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A statement that a remainder follows from a stated rule, as in arithmetic.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun it means the quantity left over after the rest has been taken away, a leftover amount.

clue.text: To the left, bend!

blocks.note: surface reading: a drill instruction to lean leftwards
setter's reading: in heraldry a bend is a diagonal band, and one running the other way across the shield takes this name

explanation.surface: A gym instructor tells the class to lean leftwards.
explanation.walkthrough: In heraldry the bend sinister is a diagonal stripe, traditionally a mark of illegitimacy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word for left survives in heraldry for the shield's left side, as seen by its bearer.

clue.text: My Jolly and I put on the guise of a classical follower

blocks.note: taken as written
a Jolly is slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM
taken as written
to don clothing is to put it on

explanation.surface: Someone and a merry companion dress up as a follower from ancient times.
explanation.walkthrough: Jolly is old naval slang for a Royal Marine, giving RM.
explanation.definitionFit: The Myrmidons were the warriors who followed Achilles in Homer's Iliad, so the word means a loyal henchman.

clue.text: Poetic hermitage to innocent minds

blocks.note: surface reading: a hermit's retreat as poets imagine it
setter's reading: Lovelace wrote that stone walls and iron bars are taken by minds innocent and quiet for a hermitage

explanation.surface: A poet's idea of a peaceful retreat for the pure in heart.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Lovelace, To Althea, from Prison: 'Stone walls do not a prison make, nor iron bars a cage; minds innocent and quiet take that for an hermitage.'
explanation.definitionFit: In the famous seventeenth-century poem, a jail cell is what untroubled minds regard as a peaceful retreat.

clue.text: Invective sounded by a group of woad users

indicators.note: sounded means spoken out, so we want words that say the same as the phrase described

blocks.note: ancient Britons painted themselves with woad, a blue dye, so such a group is a tribe that would dye

explanation.surface: Abuse shouted by a band of painted ancient Britons.
explanation.walkthrough: Woad is the blue plant dye the ancient Britons smeared on themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: A diatribe is a bitter verbal attack, and invective is abusive or violent language, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Sailor does change homes

indicators.note: to change something is to alter it, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is the usual abbreviation for a sailor
the letters of does are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sailor moves house.
explanation.definitionFit: An abode is a dwelling place, so abodes are places where people live, the same as homes.

clue.text: It is indispensable to the Latin scholar

blocks.clueFragment: It is indispensable to the Latin scholar
blocks.note: surface reading: some book or tool every classicist needs
setter's reading: the Latin phrase meaning 'without which not', i.e. something essential

explanation.surface: Something every student of Latin cannot do without.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase, literally 'without which not', is used in English for an essential condition.

clue.text: Is it cricket to be so chirpy!

definitions.text: Is it cricket to be so chirpy!

blocks.note: surface reading: the idiom 'not cricket', meaning not fair play
setter's reading: the insect called a cricket chirps by rubbing its wings together

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether it is quite sporting to be so cheerful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is it cricket' sounds like the idiom about fair play; here it is the insect itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Crickets and grasshoppers make their shrill sound by rubbing body parts together, which is the technical verb used here.

clue.text: Fireworks? What madness!

definitions.note: an exclamation; the answer as slang adjective means mad

blocks.note: first meaning: small explosive fireworks that bang
second meaning: British slang for crazy, often exclaimed

explanation.walkthrough: Christmas crackers are also the paper tubes pulled at British festive dinners; here they are bangers.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural noun names noisy explosive novelties, and the same word is informal British for insane.

clue.text: The breath of poetry

blocks.note: surface reading: the very spirit or essence of verse
setter's reading: the Latin word for a blowing or breathing upon, used for divine inspiration

explanation.surface: A lyrical phrase for the spirit that animates verse.
explanation.definitionFit: From Latin for a breathing on, the word means a sudden creative impulse, the inspiration of a poet.

clue.text: A chancy man with a rake

definitions.text: A chancy man with a rake

blocks.clueFragment: A chancy man with a rake
blocks.note: surface reading: a risky gardener, or a dodgy man who is a rake, a libertine
setter's reading: the casino official who gathers in chips with a long-handled rake at a game of chance

explanation.surface: A shady character carrying a garden tool.
explanation.walkthrough: Chancy suggests unreliable, but here means connected with games of chance.
explanation.definitionFit: The casino employee running a gaming table collects and pays out stakes using a small rake.

clue.text: They should be taken up and verified

definitions.text: They should be taken up and verified

blocks.note: surface reading: anything that should be adopted or pursued
setter's reading: an employer takes up a job applicant's referees and checks what they say

explanation.surface: Advice that some claims should be followed up and checked.
explanation.definitionFit: Testimonials from referees are routinely taken up by employers and checked before a candidate is hired.

clue.text: Jack's ecstatic when away

blocks.note: Jack, or jack tar, is a sailor, abbreviated AB
sent is old slang for thrilled or transported

explanation.surface: A man named Jack is overjoyed to be on holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone not present, gone elsewhere, is said to be missing from their usual place.

clue.text: "Full many a gem of purest ray ." (Gray)

definitions.text: "Full many a gem of purest ray ."

blocks.clueFragment: "Full many a gem of purest ray ."
blocks.note: surface reading: a line of verse with a word left out
setter's reading: Thomas Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard supplies the missing final word

explanation.walkthrough: Gray's Elegy: 'Full many a gem of purest ray serene / The dark unfathomed caves of ocean bear.'
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word completes the quotation; it means calm and clear, describing the gem's untroubled light.

clue.text: Loud strings are equal to woodwind!

blocks.note: f, forte, is the musical marking for loud
lutes are stringed instruments

explanation.surface: An orchestral joke that loud string players match the wind section.
explanation.definitionFit: These pipe-shaped instruments are members of the orchestra's wind family, played by blowing across a hole.

clue.text: It's a bit thick _ to summon America!

blocks.note: to summon is to call
US is the abbreviation for the United States

explanation.surface: Someone complains it is a bit much to call in the Americans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's a bit thick' reads as the British idiom for 'that's unreasonable', but it describes a patch of hardened skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A callus is a patch of skin that has become hardened and thickened through repeated friction.

clue.text: Stupid but devoted ' to muscular development

definitions.note: adjective here; the answer is a noun for a stupid person
describes the thing rather than naming it

blocks.note: first meaning: slang for a dim-witted person
second meaning: a short bar with weights at each end used for exercise

explanation.surface: Someone is dim but dedicated to building up their muscles.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both slang for a dull, foolish person and the name of a weighted bar lifted to build strength.

clue.text: Does it necessitate estate settlement?

blocks.note: first meaning: to involve something as an inevitable consequence
second meaning: a legal settlement restricting inheritance of property to a line of heirs

explanation.surface: A question about whether a property settlement is really required.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to involve inevitably; as a noun it is a legal arrangement fixing who inherits land.

clue.text: Advance payment?

blocks.note: surface reading: money paid before the goods or work are delivered
setter's reading: the charge paid on an advance, that is on a loan

explanation.walkthrough: Advance looks like an adjective meaning beforehand; it is a noun meaning a loan.
explanation.definitionFit: A borrower pays a lender a percentage charge on the money lent, which is the payment for a loan.

clue.text: Half - sister takes time to appear as a murder victim

blocks.note: the first half of the word sister
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A half-sister takes her time before turning up as the victim of a killing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-sister' looks like a relative; it means half the letters of sister.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Book of Judges the Canaanite general was killed by Jael, who drove a tent peg through his head.

clue.text: Addicts of colourful yarns!

blocks.note: surface reading: people who love tall stories
setter's reading: yarns are dyed wool, and these people are devoted to working it with needles

explanation.surface: People hooked on lurid tall tales.
explanation.walkthrough: A yarn is a story, but also spun wool.
explanation.definitionFit: Enthusiasts who make garments with needles from coloured wool are hooked on that thread.
